title: When do two bells ring together again?
description: One bell rings every twelve minutes and another every eighteen minutes, and they ring together now. The multiples of each are listed and the first time in both lists is found, then checked with primes. Keeko doubts this and multiplies twelve and eighteen.
teaching_notes: One idea: the first time two repeating events happen together is the lowest common multiple of their gaps. Watch for students who multiply the two numbers and so give a later time.

source: Two bells ring every 12 and 18 minutes. They ring together now. After how many minutes will they ring together again?
video_script.why: The child can find a lowest common multiple and now uses it to answer a question about two events that repeat.
video_script.substitution: List when each bell rings, find the first time in both lists, and check it with primes.
video_script.anchor: Two time lines, one for each bell, with a mark at every ring.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko multiplies twelve and eighteen to get two hundred sixteen, but both bells already ring together at thirty six.
video_script.payoff_line: The bells ring together again after thirty six minutes
never_show: 216 minutes as the first time, marked right
maths_rules: bell one rings at 12, 24, 36; bell two rings at 18, 36
the first time in both lists is 36, so it is the LCM of 12 and 18
36 = 3 × 12 and 36 = 2 × 18, so both bells ring at 36
slip: 12 × 18 = 216 is a common multiple but not the first; 216 = 6 × 36
video_script.design: One idea: the first time both bells ring is the lowest common multiple. The two time lines stay on the board.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, bell one rings at twelve, twenty four and thirty six minutes.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Bell two rings at eighteen minutes, and again at thirty six minutes.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: the first time in both lists is 36, so the LCM of 12 and 18 is 36

marks.m2: the words lowest common multiple are written beside 36

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, the first time in both lists is thirty six.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>This number, thirty six, is the lowest common multiple of twelve and eighteen.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, check with primes. Twelve is two times two times three. Eighteen is two times three times three.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The lowest common multiple takes two twos and two threes. That is thirty six.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: 36 = 3 × 12 and 36 = 2 × 18, so both bells ring at 36
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, thirty six is three twelves, so bell one rings at that time.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>It is also two eighteens, so bell two rings at that time as well.

marks.m1: the answer After 36 minutes is written and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>The bells ring together again after thirty six minutes.

narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 12 × 18 = 216 minutes; 36 is lit earlier on both time lines; 216 = 6 × 36; the bubble is struck out

marks.m2: 36 is lit on both time lines, long before 216

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks we multiply twelve and eighteen. That gives two hundred sixteen minutes.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Both bells do ring together at two hundred sixteen, but not for the first time.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Twelve and eighteen share six, so the product uses six twice.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>We need the smallest time, which is thirty six.
